articleTitle: Numerical calculation, simulation and design optimisation of claw pole alternators for automotive application
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Machines for Automotive Applications (Digest No. 1996/166)
abstract: Claw pole alternators are widely used as generators in passenger cars. They have to generate sufficient energy for all electric consumers and to keep the battery charge in balance. The present paper describes how modern design tools can be successfully applied to the optimisation of the electromagnetic design of claw pole alternators, in order to improve their output performance.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Machines for Automotive Applications (Digest No. 1996/166)
abstract: With an ever increasing amount of installed electrical load in modern automobiles there is a corresponding increase in the demands placed on the automotive electrical system. This system's inability to supply these demands efficiently at 12 V suggests that a new higher system voltage will soon become necessary. Unfortunately re-engineering, re-design and parts procurement costs prohibit a single change to a higher system voltage. A dual voltage architecture provides a simple, yet effective, solution to this problem. High demand loads such as electrically heated catalysts, heated windshields and other various heater loads can be supplied efficiently at a voltage much higher than 12 V while the traditional 12 V standard is retained to supply filament lighting, semiconductors and other loads which cannot make a transition to a higher system voltage without prohibitive consequences. The nominal output voltage of a conventional passenger car alternator is limited to 12-14 V over the entire speed range despite the fact that this voltage is initially reached at a relatively low speed. This paper describes the development of a new design of automotive alternator which allows the DC output voltage to rise to 32 V which is more suited to efficient supply of heater loads. This utilises more of the alternators output capability while retaining the traditional 12 V standard for the many other loads not suitable for higher voltage operation. Such an alternator was designed to generate and regulate two independent DC voltages within a single housing without compromising the existing 12 V system.

articleTitle: An integrated low cost sensor for the direct torque control of brushless DC motors
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Machines for Automotive Applications (Digest No. 1996/166)
abstract: Control of brushless, variable-speed drives by the use of stator field orientation techniques has received much attention in recent years and has been extensively documented. Such schemes require stator current and rotor speed or position information as inputs to a machine model which is solved for the electromagnetic torque, in real-time generally via a digital signal processor. Torque control by implementation of the above technique requires that the effects of machine parameter variations due for example, to changes in temperatures, magnetic saturation etc. and loss mechanisms due to windage, friction and parasitic effects, are taken into consideration. These nonlinearities increase the processing complexity and can result in a drive-specific controller. Also, in many industrial processors, the torque downstream in the mechanical system needs to be controlled, particularly where coupled system inertia gives rise to mechanical torsional oscillations. The alternative approach of using a discrete torque sensor as the feedback element in a torque control loop has, to date, been prohibitive on the grounds of size and cost. However, this paper presents a technical description of a new, potentially low cost noncontact torque transducer indicating surface acoustic wave (SAW) technology for shaft torque measurement. The sensor has a short axial length making it ideally suited to mounting integral with the motor housing or unobtrusively in the mechanical drive train. The operation, construction and application for torque measurement is discussed together with results from a preliminary study into the feasibility of using such a device as a transducer for control of brushless DC traction motor torque.

articleTitle: The present status of electrical machines in vehicles
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Machines for Automotive Applications (Digest No. 1996/166)
abstract: The automotive industry currently produces over 50 million vehicles worldwide with an average of 20 electrical machines giving a total production of 1 billion. Assuming an average cost of #15 per machine, the value becomes #15 billion. Electrical machines fall into three main categories: alternators-to provide power for the electrical auxiliaries; starters-for engine starting; and motors and actuators-to drive and control the wide range of auxiliaries now used on vehicles. These three categories are described in the paper.

articleTitle: Design modifications of the electrical system to use intermittent engine operation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Machines for Automotive Applications (Digest No. 1996/166)
abstract: Fuel consumption of vehicles must be minimized to reduce CO/sub 2/ emissions. Intermittent engine operation promises a high potential of improvement. Today's starter motors and alternators will not be able to fulfil the requirements for the high number of starting cycles and of the increased electric power demand. It is mandatory to improve the efficiency of all permanently operating accessories to limit the demand for electric power. It can be expected, that induction machines can serve as starter-alternator and will reach efficiencies of more than 80%.

articleTitle: Considerations in the design of small motors for automotive applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Machines for Automotive Applications (Digest No. 1996/166)
abstract: Small electric motors are used in automotive applications covering a very wide range of functions as actuators, hydraulic pumps, vacuum pumps, compressors and blowers. A selection of typical applications which would add up to about 12-15 motors on a standard car and over 50 motors on a top of range model are briefly mentioned. The basic design considerations, duty cycles, acoustic noise, EMC, safety, and quality procedures and requirements are briefly discussed.

articleTitle: Limited motion actuators for automotive applications
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Machines for Automotive Applications (Digest No. 1996/166)
abstract: Electromechanical limited motion linear actuators are playing an increasingly important role in electrohydraulic automotive systems. A detailed understanding of the transient field distribution within the actuator and the influence of material properties and the geometry of the moving member is a clear pre-requisite to reliably predicting the dynamic performance of any electromechanical actuation system, which in turn facilitates design optimisation including the selection of the most appropriate magnetic materials to meet a given performance specification. To this end, a comprehensive dynamic system simulation facility has been developed, which is based around the calculation of the transient magnetic field distribution by nonlinear finite element analysis and the simultaneous solution of the coupled equations governing electrical drive circuit and the coupled mechanical system.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Machines for Automotive Applications (Digest No. 1996/166)
abstract: Increased customer pressure and corresponding increase in vehicle sophistication dictates the need for local intelligence at the actuator. Here, the authors describe how the existing use of data bus systems provides the ability to pass information directly to the actuator. The use of electronic control can lead to reduced actuator size. Links to and use of external or internal sensors can also be incorporated. An example of a newly developed anti-theft system for diesel engine vehicles is also presented.
